ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: The figure below is a pedigree chart of a certain genetic disease. It is known that the disease-causing gene is located on the X chromosome. Question: If II-3 has another son, what is the probability that he will be affected?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In generation I of the pedigree in the figure, I-1 is a black square, indicating an affected male; I-2 is a white circle, indicating a normal female. Among the offspring born to the two, II-3 is a black circle, indicating an affected female. II-3 is connected with II-4; II-4 is a white square, indicating a normal male; they already have a white-circle daughter and a black-square son. The stem states that the disease-causing gene is located on the X chromosome. Then reason: According to the manifestation in the figure that the daughter II-3 born to affected male I-1 and normal female I-2 is affected and the son can be normal, it can be analyzed as X-linked dominant inheritance. II-3 obtains the X chromosome carrying the disease-causing gene from the affected father I-1 and obtains a normal X chromosome from the normal mother I-2, so II-3 is a heterozygous affected female. If II-3 gives birth to another son, the son's Y chromosome comes from father II-4, and the X chromosome can only come from mother II-3. Heterozygous II-3 has a 1/2 probability of passing the disease-causing X to the son, so the probability that the son is affected is 1/2.
